entries.clue: Clobber team denied opening, game displaying this? (3-2-3-2)

annotation.definitionNote: The clue never offers a synonym: 'this' points back at the entry itself, and the solver has to supply what a game player is displaying, which the question mark admits is vague.

indicatorNotes.denied opening: To be denied something is to have it withheld, and the opening of a word is the letter it starts with.

blocks.note: clobber is British slang for someone's clothes, the same sense as an outfit or a rig-out
a band is a team of people, and the letter it opens with, B, is withheld
the ancient board game of black and white stones

annotation.surface: A team turned out in full kit and denied the opening of the game.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Clobber' looks like the verb for hitting and is the noun, British slang for clothes. The definition is the tail of the clue pointing back at itself: what somebody game displays is left for the solver to name.
annotation.definitionFit: Get-up-and-go is the drive and initiative a person visibly has, so the clue asks who is showing it rather than offering a word for it.

blocks.note: the parcel handed over on a birthday
a natural aptitude, the kind someone is said to be born with

annotation.surface: The talent on show at the moment.
annotation.walkthrough: Two bare nouns side by side is the double definition's usual shape. 'Present' reads first as the adjective for current, which is what makes the pair look like one phrase rather than two clues.
annotation.definitionFit: A present is the wrapped thing itself, and the same word covers a natural talent — the sense behind calling someone gifted.

annotation.definitionNote: The verb 'Made' is shared by both halves — made haste, and made a ladder — so the second definition only agrees with the answer's past tense once the reader carries that verb across the dash.

blocks.note: the past tense of a verb for going at speed, as in ripping down the road
in Britain a ladder is the run that opens up a pair of tights, and it is made by tearing them

annotation.surface: Someone rushing off and wrecking their tights on the way.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A ladder' wants to be the thing you climb, and it is the run up a stocking. The single verb at the front has to be read twice for the two halves to meet.
annotation.definitionFit: To tear off somewhere is to go at speed, and tights that have torn have laddered — the British word for the run that appears in them.

indicatorNotes.up: On a down entry, up means the letters climb the column, so the word is read from its last letter to its first.

blocks.note: the lowest rank in the army, the ordinary soldier of the ranks
a moor is open upland, heather and peat, and its four letters are taken the other way about

annotation.surface: A soldier tying a boat up on a quiet stretch of water.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Moor up' reads as making a boat fast to the bank, which hides both the open heath and the instruction to climb. The soldier is the rank, not somebody keeping a secret.
annotation.definitionFit: A private room is one nobody else is in — the quiet corner of a pub or a hospital where you are left undisturbed.

entries.clue: Primarily: naturally / oh, so what / easy / any time? (2,5)

annotation.definition: Primarily: naturally / oh, so what / easy / any time?

indicatorNotes.Primarily: Primarily means at the very start, so each item on the list gives up only the letter it begins with.

blocks.clueFragment: naturally / oh, so what / easy / any time?
blocks.note: seven words in the order printed, each handing over its opening letter

annotation.surface: A list of breezy things people say when they are waving away a favour.
annotation.walkthrough: Each item on the list is something a person says instead of the answer, and the very same words spell it from their front letters — both jobs at once, which is what &lit means.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: naturally, so what, easy and any time are all ways of saying a thing cost you nothing at all.

entries.clue: Gentleman to drive away, we're told, in casual footwear (3,4)

indicatorNotes.we're told: What we are told we hear rather than read, so both words beside it are wanted for their sound and get written down another way.

blocks.note: the gentleman here is a man with a name, and Gentleman Jim — the boxer James Corbett — is the pairing the ear reaches for
to shoo is to wave something off, as you would a cat off a table

annotation.surface: A gentleman waving somebody away, reportedly wearing something soft on his feet.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves are heard rather than spelt, with one instruction covering the pair, which is rarer than a single sound. A gym shoe is the plimsoll a British school pupil keeps in a drawstring bag.
annotation.definitionFit: A gym shoe is the soft canvas plimsoll worn for sport and lounging about — footwear at the informal end of the rack.

indicatorNotes.in retrospective: Retrospective means looking back over what has gone, and on an across entry looking back is reading the letters from the right-hand end.

blocks.note: a celebrated hero is a much-sung one, and those four letters are written back to front

annotation.surface: An artist honoured by an exhibition looking back over the work.
annotation.walkthrough: A retrospective is a gallery show of an artist's past work, which is where the surface wants the eye. 'Celebrated' is the adjective in its older sense, sung about.
annotation.definitionFit: Gnus are the wildebeest of the African plains, the bearded antelope that cross the Serengeti in vast herds.

indicatorNotes.Vain: Vain works twice over: of the man it means conceited, and as an instruction it is the empty, come-to-nothing sense, warning that the letters beside it stand for nothing in the order given.

blocks.note: ten letters of raw material, the apostrophe ignored

annotation.surface: A conceited man having some sort of breakdown.
annotation.walkthrough: Read straight it names a condition, and the same three words are also its letters, which is what &lit means. The word comes from Narcissus, the Greek youth who fell in love with his own reflection.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: narcissism is what a vain man's crisis consists of, self-love grown into the problem itself.

indicatorNotes.up: Up here is the sense in mixed up or shaken up, disorder rather than height, so the letters before it do not stay as they are.

blocks.note: ten letters of raw material

annotation.surface: A little bird's shorts pegged out on the washing line.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hung up' wants to be read as one phrase, and the instruction is the last word standing alone. This bird repeats each phrase of its song two or three times, which is how you tell it from a blackbird.
annotation.definitionFit: A song thrush sings long and loudly from a high perch, so 'warbler' is the everyday sense of a bird that warbles rather than the warbler family proper.

entries.clue: Because, quaintly, it is mostly Paul singing loudly (10)

indicatorNotes.quaintly: Quaintly asks for the old-fashioned way of putting it, the contraction met in ballads rather than in speech.
indicatorNotes.mostly: Mostly means nearly all of it, so the name arrives with its final letter left off.

blocks.note: for and because do the same job joining two halves of a sentence
'tis is the old contraction of it is
the singer is Paul Simon, and all but the last letter of that surname is wanted

annotation.surface: Explaining that the voice you can hear is mostly Paul, belting it out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Paul singing' asks for the surname rather than the first name — Paul Simon. The answer is the mark a composer writes over a bar, ff, telling the performer to give it everything.
annotation.definitionFit: Fortissimo is the direction to perform very loudly, the superlative of forte, so it drops straight into 'singing loudly'.

entries.clue: Architect who creates home from moss (4)

blocks.note: Sir Christopher, who rebuilt St Paul's Cathedral and fifty City churches after the Great Fire of London
the bird weaves a domed nest of moss and leaves, tucked into a bank or a wall

annotation.surface: An architect who can make a house out of almost nothing.
annotation.walkthrough: Nothing in the clue signals the switch from the man to the bird, and the relative pronoun keeps both readings alive. Sir Christopher Wren's name is on half the churches in the City of London.
annotation.definitionFit: Sir Christopher Wren is the architect the bare word points at, and the wren is the tiny brown bird that builds its nest out of moss.

entries.clue: Cover roast with foil and plan a crime? (4,3,5)

blocks.note: to case something is to put a case round it, the way a pillow is cased
a joint is the cut of meat that goes in the oven on a Sunday, and the phrase brings its definite article with it
what you would cover a roast with; it is there for the kitchen picture and hands over no letters

annotation.surface: Wrapping the Sunday roast in foil before it goes in the oven.
annotation.walkthrough: The kitchen reading of the wordplay is exact, foil and all, which is why nothing in it feels like instructions. Burglars' slang keeps the same two nouns and changes what both of them mean.
annotation.definitionFit: To case the joint is thieves' slang for sizing up a building before breaking into it, which is planning the crime rather than committing it.

entries.clue: With seconds to spare, just damn edgy, worried it's the end of the world (8,3)

indicatorNotes.to spare: What is spare is over and above what is needed, so the letter named beside it is set aside and takes no part in the rest.
indicatorNotes.worried: A worried person cannot keep still, and letters worried the same way will not stay in the order they are given.

blocks.note: s is the standard shorthand for seconds, as printed on a stopwatch
twelve letters of raw material, one more than the grid has room for
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Someone arriving with seconds to spare, edgy and certain that disaster is coming.
annotation.walkthrough: 'With seconds to spare' reads as the clock and is the instruction to drop a letter before anything else happens. Judgment takes its shorter spelling here, with no e in the middle, which the crossings confirm.
annotation.definitionFit: Judgment Day is the Last Judgment of Christian belief, when the world ends and everybody is called to account.

indicatorNotes.cured: To cure something is to treat it until it has turned into something that keeps, and the letters beside it are treated the same way.

blocks.note: ten letters of raw material, the colon ignored

annotation.surface: A dream in which everything on the table is charcuterie.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cured' sits exactly where a solver reads it as part of the meat, and it is the instruction. The answer is the big pink Bologna sausage, studded with white fat, that Americans turned into baloney.
annotation.definitionFit: Mortadella is a cured pork sausage from Bologna, so the bare word 'meat' defines it by kind.

annotation.definitionNote: Lingerie is a collective word for women's underclothes and has no plural of its own, so it defines a plural garment name without matching its -s.

indicatorNotes.shredded: Shredded means torn into pieces, and letters in pieces can be laid down in any order you like.

blocks.note: ten letters of raw material

annotation.surface: A cat taking its revenge on somebody's underwear.
annotation.walkthrough: The cat doing the shredding is the picture and the same word is the instruction, which is why it reads as scenery. A petticoat is the underskirt worn beneath a dress.
annotation.definitionFit: Petticoats are underskirts worn next to the skin, which puts them squarely in the lingerie drawer.

entries.clue: After deliveries, with just the starters, Everyman's apt to indulge (7)

indicatorNotes.After: After puts what follows behind the piece already named, so the letters gathered later sit at the back.
indicatorNotes.with just the starters: Starters are what begin things, so only the letter each word starts with is taken.

blocks.note: in cricket an over is the set of six deliveries bowled from one end
the first letter of each of those three words, in the order they stand

annotation.surface: Once the bowling is done, Everyman is likely to make a meal of the starters.
annotation.walkthrough: Everyman writes himself into his own clues, so his name is material rather than scenery. 'Starters' is doing two jobs at once: the first course on the table and the first letters of the words.
annotation.definitionFit: To overeat is to eat more than you should, which is what indulging at the table amounts to.

indicatorNotes.supply: Supply is the adverb from supple, said SUP-lee — in a limber, bending way — and letters that bend take whatever shape is asked of them.

blocks.note: seven letters of raw material

annotation.surface: A guaranteed supply reaching whoever is buying.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Supply' looks like the noun holding up a sentence about deliveries, and it is the adverb from supple. An end user is whoever finally uses a product, as distinct from whoever bought or sold it.
annotation.definitionFit: The end user is the person at the end of the chain who actually uses the thing, which is the customer a supplier is selling to.

annotation.definitionNote: Needlework is a mass noun naming the whole craft, so it has no plural of its own to set against the answer's several pieces of work.

blocks.note: the needle going in and out, here of skin rather than cloth
the evening show of massed bands, from the Dutch doe den tap toe, 'turn off the taps', the drumbeat that sent soldiers home from the inns

annotation.surface: Embroidery on show at an army pageant.
annotation.walkthrough: The needle joins the two senses by accident only: the military one comes from the Dutch call that closed the taverns at night. The Edinburgh Tattoo on the castle esplanade is the famous one.
annotation.definitionFit: Tattoos are inked into the skin with needles, and a military tattoo is the ceremonial evening display of marching and massed bands.

entries.clue: New Orleans: it's SE of Naples (7)

indicatorNotes.New: New asks for the letters made over into something they were not, which here is a fresh arrangement of the ones already there.

blocks.note: seven letters of raw material

annotation.surface: Somebody placing New Orleans on the map, southeast of Naples.
annotation.walkthrough: The Naples wanted is the Italian one, though there is a Naples in Florida that almost makes the geography of the surface work. The answer is the port where the Allies landed in September 1943.
annotation.definitionFit: Salerno is the Italian port on the gulf of the same name, thirty miles down the coast southeast of Naples.

entries.clue: Flipping sibling with sound that's meditative, very - it permeates gradually (7)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a sentence about the answer rather than a synonym for it: 'it' stands in for the process, so a verb phrase does the work a noun would.

indicatorNotes.Flipping: To flip something is to turn it over, so the letters just assembled are read back from the far end.

blocks.note: the familiar short form for a sister
om is the syllable chanted in Hindu and Buddhist meditation
so tired means very tired

annotation.surface: An exasperating sibling humming something very meditative indeed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' is the mild British swear word in the surface and the turn-around instruction in the answer. Picking something up by osmosis is the everyday use: absorbing it without ever being taught.
annotation.definitionFit: Osmosis is water passing slowly through a membrane, and the word is used of anything that seeps in by degrees rather than arriving at once.

indicatorNotes.Somewhat: Somewhat asks for a part and not the whole, and the part wanted runs unbroken through the words beside it.

blocks.note: the letters run straight on across the three words, beginning at the last letter of the Spanish adjective

annotation.surface: Somebody scoffing at an extravagantly ornate Spanish baroque style.
annotation.walkthrough: Churrigueresco is Spanish for the wildly ornate baroque of the Churriguera family, all twisted columns and gilt — a style as overblown as the word being defined. Short exclamations in a row are a favourite hiding place.
annotation.definitionFit: Orotund describes speech that is round, full and pompous, which is exactly the magniloquent manner.

blocks.note: read straight, a stain or a blemish; read the setter's way, a mark of notation
read straight, shunned by coarse people; read the setter's way, unused by vulgar fractions, which write a half as 1/2

annotation.surface: Something the coarser sort of person would never be caught using.
annotation.walkthrough: A vulgar fraction is the ordinary sort written as one number over another, and the whole of its method is managing without the other notation. 'Eschewed' is a mannered word for avoided, which sets the snobbish tone.
annotation.definitionFit: A decimal point is the dot dividing whole from fractional parts, and vulgar fractions do their work without one.

indicatorNotes.loud: Loud asks to be heard rather than read: the word beside it is wanted for its sound, and the spelling that arrives is a different one.

blocks.note: a ribbon tied in a knot is a bow, and that is said exactly as the answer is

annotation.surface: A young man's showy ribbon.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Loud' reads as garish, the sort of ribbon you would notice across a room, and it is the instruction to listen instead. The word for a woman's admirer is eighteenth-century and survives mostly in novels.
annotation.definitionFit: A beau is a lady's sweetheart or admirer, the man paying court to her, which is what a suitor does.

indicatorNotes.in: In points inside the word that follows: what is wanted sits within it rather than being described by it.

blocks.note: four consecutive letters of the word, beginning at the third

annotation.surface: A party held down on the seafront.
annotation.walkthrough: A 'do' is British for a party as well as for a hairstyle, and the surface leans on the party. One long word on its own is an easy place to miss an answer sitting in plain sight.
annotation.definitionFit: A do is British shorthand for a hairstyle — the hairdo — and an afro is one, grown out into a rounded mass.

blocks.note: the dull grey metal of church roofs and old plumbing, famous for its weight
the part with the most lines in it, and the actor given it

annotation.surface: A star of heavy metal music.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Heavy metal' reads as the music and turns out to be two words doing their literal work. The two senses are not even said alike, led and leed, which a grid of capital letters happily conceals.
annotation.definitionFit: Lead is the heaviest of the common metals, and the lead in a film or a play is the star part.

entries.clue: Argue, with justification, for what goes into burger (6,4)

blocks.note: a ground for doing something is the reason that justifies it
to beef is to complain, and a beef is the grievance itself

annotation.surface: Making a case, with good reason, for what a burger should contain.
annotation.walkthrough: The wordplay assembles as a complaint with grounds — the justification in front, the grumble behind — which is why the pieces come out the other way round from the clue. The answer is the American name for what a British butcher calls mince.
annotation.definitionFit: Ground beef is minced beef, which is what the patty in a burger is made of.

blocks.note: Al Capone is the crossword's gangster, and the apostrophe-s comes along as a letter
love is nothing in tennis, written as a nought

annotation.surface: A mobster's sweetheart.
annotation.walkthrough: The possessive s is a letter rather than punctuation, which is allowed: a setter's apostrophes never bind the solver. 'Love' is the tennis scoreboard's zero.
annotation.definitionFit: Also does the job of and when one thing is added to another: he sings, and he also dances.

blocks.note: the formal greeting on being introduced, answered by repeating it straight back
a fine one of these, in the old phrase, is an awkward state of affairs

annotation.walkthrough: Two words and no joinery at all is the barest double definition there is. The second sense nearly always turns up dressed as 'a fine how-do-you-do', meaning a mess somebody has landed in.
annotation.definitionFit: How-do-you-do is the formal greeting made on being introduced, and the same phrase names a commotion or a muddle.
